title: Recursion and divide-and-conquer
lead: Prove the base case is reachable, trace returns and construct a stable merge over bounded input.
why: Recursion is useful when a problem splits into smaller problems of the same form. It does not automatically make code simple or fast: account for call state, combination cost and runtime limits.
objectives: Prove termination with a decreasing measure.
Separate stack depth and buffer size.
prerequisites: Modules 1–3: validated input, functions, vector, records, references and lifetimes.
Direct learning dependencies: cpp.search-linear-binary, cpp.functions-contracts. New constructs are explained before the task.

concepts.definition: A simple case that ends a branch without another call.
A nonnegative quantity decreasing strictly before a recursive step.
Separate parameters and local objects for one invocation.
The maximum simultaneously active calls along one branch.
Splitting a problem into smaller subproblems.
Combining two ordered ranges in linear work.
Relating problem cost to subproblem and combination costs.

sections.title: A call preserves a continuation
paragraphs: A recursive function calls itself directly or through other functions. Each call has its own parameters and local objects. In factorial(4), 4·factorial(3) remains unfinished until the inner result returns. A trace must therefore show both descent 4→3→2→1 and return values 1→2→6→24.

A conventional implementation stores continuation state on a call stack. This is not the std::stack container from the previous module: calls are managed by the language/runtime, while the container holds application data. Never return a reference to a local object whose call has ended. Mutate a live external vector through a reference and pass subproblem bounds as values.

sections.title: A base case and a progress measure
paragraphs: A base case produces its answer without another recursive call. Factorial returns one at zero and one. A sort needs no work on a range shorter than two. Handle the base case before operations requiring an element: an empty range has no a[0], though sorting it is valid.

The progress measure must strictly decrease within a well-founded domain. For factorial(n−1) at n≥2 it is n; for merge sort it is hi−lo. Checking n<0 before conversion to unsigned is essential, or a negative input becomes a large positive value and changes the argument. “It will stop eventually” is not a named progress measure.

sections.title: Induction connects a local step to the answer
paragraphs: Assume a call correctly solves a smaller problem. Then multiplying n by a correct factorial(n−1) gives factorial(n), provided arithmetic is valid. This is the inductive step; the base case anchors it. Assuming correctness for a problem of the same size is circular and supplies no termination proof.

For merge sort the assumption covers two smaller ranges. After they return, merging still needs its own proof: correct halves do not guarantee the next item is chosen correctly. Separate valid splitting, correct smaller solutions and correct combination preserving every item.

sections.title: Splitting and the call tree
paragraphs: Use [lo,hi) and mid=lo+(hi−lo)/2. At length at least two, both halves are smaller. Their lengths can differ by one: seven items split into three and four. Draw the size tree 7→(3,4) down to singletons; empty and singleton leaves use the base case.

The lab numbers the root depth as one, including an empty input. maximum is the deepest executed call, not the total number of calls. For 128 items it is eight, following from balanced splitting and that numbering convention. This small experiment does not determine the browser’s maximum stack capacity.

sections.title: Merging two prepared fronts
paragraphs: After sorting the halves, i and j identify their first unconsumed items. The invariant says tmp holds the smallest items already selected in order, while both remainders remain sorted. Compare their fronts and append the smaller. When one half is exhausted, append the other remainder in its existing order.

Choose the left half on ties when stability is required. The code tests right<left first and otherwise selects left. tmp then has hi−lo items and copies back to the same range. Do not read a[i] at i==mid or a[j] at j==hi; boundary checks precede the comparison.

sections.title: Recurrence cost and memory
paragraphs: Merging n bounded integers takes linear work. T(n)=T(⌊n/2⌋)+T(⌈n/2⌉)+Θ(n) gives Θ(n log n): each level processes about n items in total and there are about log n levels. This is a level-by-level argument, not a deduction from one timing graph.

Here tmp is created after both child calls return. Peak auxiliary-buffer space is O(n), with O(log n) active call frames. Repeated allocation still affects constants; a shared workspace buffer is a separate design option. Total allocated bytes over a run and maximum simultaneously occupied memory are different metrics.

sections.title: Depth, repeated work and bounded rejection
paragraphs: Not every recursion is balanced. Splitting n into n−1 and one gives linear depth, while naive Fibonacci repeats identical subproblems many times. Estimate both call count and path depth before choosing recursion. Iteration or an explicit work stack may be preferable when depth follows potentially large input.

The lab rejects n>128 before sorting; the factorial example is limited to 12. These are documented educational bounds, not an ability to process every input. Do not promise tail-call elimination as a required guarantee of ordinary C++ code. Timeouts and stack exhaustion should not be your main precondition checks.

sections.title: Traces, tests and transfer
paragraphs: Draw the call tree for n=3, then a return trace showing the halves being merged. Test empty, singleton, odd-length, reverse, duplicate and maximum-size data. Validate maximum under the stated root-depth-one convention. Check multiset preservation separately: a correct depth says nothing about preserved values.

Extend values with original labels and demonstrate stability on tied keys. Compare local and shared-buffer space without calling an assumption a measurement. Next, choose containers for key-based queries; a container’s potentially recursive implementation does not replace understanding its public contract.

workedExamples.title: Factorial: base case, progress and a bound
workedExamples.purpose: Compare recursion with an independent iterative computation over a bounded domain.
steps: Validate 0…12 before converting to unsigned; a negative input must not silently become a large value.
At 0 or 1 the function returns 1 without another call.
For 5, factorial(4) is evaluated first; return-time multiplications produce 2, 6, 24, 120.
Each call decreases n, so the base case is reachable; uint64_t and the bound 12 avoid overflow here.
Agreement with a loop checks the result, not equal memory use or guaranteed tail-call elimination.

workedExamples.title: Split, solve, combine
workedExamples.purpose: Separate merge correctness from the recursion-depth bound.
steps: [0,6) splits into [0,3) and [3,6), then repeatedly splits down to lengths zero or one.
After both calls return, each half is sorted by the induction hypothesis.
Choose the smaller first remaining item; ties go to the left half.
Append the remainder of the nonempty half and copy the temporary buffer back.
This bounded experiment checks an oracle and maximum<=8; it does not measure the maximum WASI stack.

laboratory.title: Laboratory: Recursion and divide-and-conquer
laboratory.catalogGoal: Prove the base case is reachable, trace returns and construct a stable merge over bounded input.
laboratory.challenge: Read n in 0…128 and n integers in −10000…10000 with no extra tokens. Sort using recursive merge sort. First line: space-separated values; second: max-depth D. Root depth is 1, with base n<2. Invalid input produces only invalid.
steps: Restate the input domain, format, bounds and rejection policy.
First implement complete input validation without partial results.
Implement merge sort under the lab contract.
Run all reference cases; for files check existence and content too.
Save the source, observed-results table and invariant explanation; add an independent case.

assessment.question: Merge-sort base case?
assessment.explanation: An empty range must terminate too.

assessment.question: A termination measure?
assessment.explanation: Both child lengths are smaller for n>=2.

assessment.question: Depth at n=0 under the contract?
assessment.explanation: The root invocation counts even on empty input.

assessment.question: Stable merge on equality?
assessment.explanation: The left record originally occurred earlier.

assessment.question: Balanced T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n) gives…
assessment.explanation: Each of O(log n) levels performs O(n) work.
